title: Nanak on the mountain
hook: Bhai Gurdas tells of the yogis on Mount Sumer asking Nanak about the world below (Bhai Gurdas, Var 1)

segments.voice: Yesterday, your line was the mist cleared. Did the fog lift off someone you'd stopped seeing? Today the light goes climbing. Day seven hundred one.

So, how are things down there? It's the question you ask someone who's just come in from outside, when you've been indoors all day. In Bhai Gurdas's first var, it's asked on a mountain. Guru Nanak climbs up to Sumer, and the siddhs are there, yogis who have left the world far below them to practice in the heights. They see him arrive, and they ask him for news. Year one told what Nanak said to yogis about living in the world. Today, Bhai Gurdas's version of the question, and the answer he remembers. Today: Nanak on the mountain.
screen: `SO, HOW ARE THINGS DOWN THERE?` → `THE SIDDHS ON SUMER.` → `NANAK ON THE MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: In Bhai Gurdas's telling, the siddhs ask Nanak what's happening in the world of mortals, the world below. It's a polite question, maybe a curious one. And Nanak's answer is not polite small talk. He says truth has become like a moon that can't be seen, and falsehood like a moonless dark. He says he has gone out searching through that dark. And then he turns the question around. The siddhs, he says, have gone and hidden in the mountains. So who is going to carry the world across? There's an edge to that. The yogis asked about the world below as if it were somewhere else, somebody else's problem, interesting news from far away. Nanak answers as if they're part of the story: the people best trained in stillness and discipline have climbed out of reach, just when the world needs them. Bhai Gurdas is not mocking the siddhs' discipline. He takes it seriously, which is why the question bites. Training means something because of what it's for. Holiness, in this telling, doesn't belong up on the mountain looking down. It belongs back in the valley, with the farmers, the traders, the families, the people living in the dark. Which is where Nanak himself is going: tomorrow to Mecca, and soon, home to Kartarpur. The mountain is a place to visit. The world below is where the work is.
screen: `WHAT'S HAPPENING IN THE WORLD BELOW?` · `TRUTH LIKE A HIDDEN MOON.` · `WHO WILL CARRY THE WORLD ACROSS?` · `THE WORK IS IN THE VALLEY.` · then, large: `WHAT OF THE WORLD BELOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look down from somewhere high. It doesn't have to be a mountain. The top of a staircase, an upstairs window, a balcony, a hill, even standing on the step outside your door. Look down at the street, the yard, the people passing. Then ask the siddhs' question honestly: what is happening down there? Who is struggling? Who is waiting for someone to come back down? Let one face or one place come to mind. If you pray, you can hold that person in the Name for the rest of the sit. The bell holds the time.
Nanak on the mountain. Bhai Gurdas's telling of the siddhs asking for news of the world below, and Nanak asking back who will carry that world across.
Your line: what of the world below. Today, come down from one comfortable height: answer the message you've been avoiding, or check on the person you keep meaning to. Day seven hundred one.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Nanak's meetings with the siddhs, told by Bhai Gurdas and in the Siddh Gosht of the Guru Granth Sahib, as a call to live a holy life within the world rather than withdrawing from it.

he asks who will carry the world across while they hide in the mountains.

fork.setup: you're Nanak, standing among yogis high on the mountain. they ask, kindly, for news of the world below. what do you say?
options: all is well; stay where you are.
it's dark down there, and you've gone to hide. who will carry it across?
nothing, and stay up here with them.
fork.reveal: in Bhai Gurdas's telling, Nanak says truth is hidden like the moon, and asks who will carry the world across while the siddhs hide in the mountains.

trapdoor: what you thought: yogis asking a traveler for the news.
what it means: Nanak answers that the world is dark, and the people trained to help have climbed out of reach.
what a scholar hears: Bhai Gurdas tells it in a few stanzas; the Guru Granth Sahib has its own long dialogue with the siddhs, the Siddh Gosht, beginning on Ang 938.

sources.ref: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Var 1, pauris 28–29 (Nanak on Sumer; the siddhs' question)
Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 938 (Ramkali, Siddh Gosht, opening)

notes: Var 1 pauris 28–29 paraphrased from memory: the siddhs ask what is happening in the mortal world; Nanak answers that truth is a moon not seen and falsehood darkness, that he set out searching, and that the siddhs have hidden in the mountains, so who will carry the world across. Confirm the pauri numbers and the paraphrase.
Year 1 day 39 ('The yogis on the mountain') covered the Siddh Gosht theme of living in the world unstained; this day keeps to Bhai Gurdas's question-and-answer to avoid repeating it.
Siddh Gosht opening at Ang 938: confirm.
Mount Sumer is named as in the var; no claims about its location are made.
